narrative:
Your application was denied because the model predicts a 64% chance that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. In plain terms, this means that, based on the academic signals in your record, you are more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam, and the law school judged that risk too high to admit you.

The single most important factor in this decision was your class standing in your third year. You finished in the bottom decile of your school, while accepted students typically landed around the middle decile. This was the strongest signal pushing the prediction toward bar exam failure, because your academic position in your final year suggests serious difficulty mastering legal material. Your first-year class standing was also low, further reinforcing that pattern.

The second most influential factor was your LSAT score. Your score of 20 is well below the average of about 37 for accepted students. This matters because the LSAT measures reasoning skills that are directly related to bar exam performance, so a low score substantially raised your predicted chance of failing.

Interestingly, your undergraduate GPA was not part of the problem. Even though your 2.70 GPA is below the accepted student average of 3.23, this factor actually pushed slightly toward passing. It did not outweigh the other two, but it shows you have academic ability that is not reflected in your law school performance.

To improve your chances, focus on retaking the LSAT after serious preparation and consider strengthening your academic record through additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate program. A higher LSAT score and a better final-year class standing would directly address the reasons your application was denied.
